metadata.title: Objective data-driven personalised approach to diagnosis of chronic tinnitus: the Tinnitus Detection (TIDE) project – protocol for the identification and validation of a biomarker for tinnitus

sections.text: Abstract Background Tinnitus is the perception of sound without an external source, often considered a phantom percept similar to phantom limb sensations, resulting from maladaptive plasticity in the brain. The condition lacks an established biomarker for diagnosis but recent studies have linked it to neural changes. The Tinnitus Detection consortium aims to identify and validate potential biomarkers for tinnitus presence and intensity. Methods/design This multicentre prospective case–control study will recruit 560 adults (280 chronic tinnitus; 280 controls). Participants will complete standardised audiological and questionnaire assessments and then undergo 64-channel electroencephalography (and magnetoencephalography at one site) to record event-related potentials during (1) a cortical gap prepulse inhibition of the acoustic startle (GPIAS) paradigm assessing gap-related inhibition of the N1 response and (2) an omission auditory oddball paradigm quantifying mismatch negativity and P300 as candidate biomarkers of tinnitus presence and loudness. Discussion The identification of a biomarker for tinnitus is crucial for developing personalised diagnosis and treatment: There is a need for updated guidelines and more effective tinnitus treatments, as existing interventions often rely on subjective measures. The success of biomarkers like GPIAS and oddball paradigms could significantly improve the reliability of tinnitus diagnosis and treatment, marking a transformative step in the field. Trial registration number NCT06520865 .

Tinnitus is an individual’s perception of sound(s) without an external source, 1 and more specifically, without a correlated acoustic or mechanical signal in the sensory organ of hearing—the cochlea. 2 Tinnitus can be triggered by multiple causes, 3 but in general, is considered a phantom percept mimicking the principles of phantom limb sensation after amputation, 4 where the lack of sensory input causes the brain to compensate for the missing input when deemed salient 4 via a phenomenon called maladaptive plasticity. 5 6 Tinnitus has a global prevalence of 14.4%, the severe form of tinnitus being 2.3% 7 having a major impact on life quality and an increased risk for suicidal ideation. 8 In addition, tinnitus is associated with psychiatric symptoms—particularly depression and anxiety—which can further exacerbate quality-of-life impairment. 9 Although considerable advances have been made in understanding the mechanisms of tinnitus, the clinical management of tinnitus remains largely based on a ‘trial and error’ approach. In everyday practice, tinnitus is typically diagnosed from the patient’s report, and clinicians must first differentiate primary subjective tinnitus from tinnitus secondary to identifiable otological, neurological or vascular conditions (eg, objective or heartbeat-synchronous tinnitus), as well as from presentations in which non-auditory factors substantially shape symptom expression. In addition, psychiatric symptoms such as anxiety and depression frequently co-occur with tinnitus and can modulate tinnitus-related distress and perceived severity, independently of the underlying auditory profile. This heterogeneity complicates differential diagnosis and contributes to variability in treatment response. An objective biomarker could therefore complement clinical assessment by providing a quantifiable signal of tinnitus presence and/or intensity, improving diagnostic confidence and enabling more accurate stratification for treatment selection and trials. Whereas it is largely agreed that, at present, there are no established, objective, quantitative and translationally valid biomarkers for diagnosing and characterising tinnitus (ringing in the ears), 10 recent studies have started to tackle various means of stratifying individuals with tinnitus. For instance, due to its strong relationship with hearing loss, it has been long debated whether tinnitus-related pathological alterations can be found in the ear or in the brain, or are different between patients with and without hearing loss. 11 Notably, beyond pure-tone thresholds, tinnitus has also been associated with poorer speech comprehension: recent work reported that speech recognition thresholds correlate with tinnitus intensity and that tinnitus-related speech comprehension difficulties may be present even when pure-tone audiometric thresholds are normal, further underscoring the complexity of tinnitus. 12 While the auditory system is central to tinnitus pathophysiology, emerging evidence also suggests that systemic factors may also contribute to tinnitus risk and severity. 13 Recent large studies demonstrated that once constant, tinnitus correlates with neural changes at least in the midbrain, 14 supporting the notion that robust neural biomarkers for tinnitus may be identified. 15 16 In contrast, no specific biomarkers have been found in the blood plasma from individuals with constant tinnitus. 17 Similarly, when severe, tinnitus is associated with genetic variants related to synaptic plasticity 18 and large-scale cortical network changes. 19 While some of these biomarkers may be helpful in stratifying tinnitus into subtypes, they are neither appropriate for diagnosing tinnitus nor for the quantification of a treatment outcome. In this regard, the development of an objective and quantifiable measure of tinnitus, which can be reliably obtained in a clinical environment, would be an important milestone for the tinnitus field. The value of such a biomarker would be significant by (1) enticing the pharmaceutical and hearing technology industry requirements to start investing in tinnitus, (2) facilitating translational research, (3) reducing risks associated with inappropriate treatment regimens or an inability to detect efficacy rapidly, and (4) leading to a marked reduction in one of the patients’ biggest frustrations of not being ‘taken seriously’, as they cannot prove they have tinnitus. 20

The objective of the Tinnitus Detection (TIDE) project is to identify and validate neurophysiological biomarkers of chronic tinnitus using standardised paradigms across multiple international sites. Primary aim: To determine whether electroencephalography (EEG)/magnetoencephalographic (MEG) event-related potential markers derived from (1) cortical gap prepulse inhibition of the acoustic startle (GPIAS) and (2) an omission auditory oddball paradigm can differentiate individuals with chronic tinnitus from matched controls. Secondary aims:

The study is designed as a multicentre, prospective, case-control, experimental and patient-oriented study aimed at collecting a large sample of data from 560 participants (ie, 280 chronic and constant tinnitus cases and 280 non-tinnitus controls) at seven sites (Tinnitus Clinics at the University Hospital Regensburg (Principal Investigator (PI): BL), Germany; University Clinic of Tübingen (PI: CRC), Germany; Brai3n clinic, Belgium; Trinity College Dublin, Ireland (TCD; PI: SV), Ireland; University of Zurich (UZH; PI: WS), Switzerland; University of Texas at Austin (UTA; PI: JC), 7 USA; University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign (PI: FTH), USA; see figure 1 ). Involvement of patient and public representatives has not been used in the study design, however PPI occurred during the evaluation of the funding.
The study started on 1 August 2024 and recruitment is scheduled to be completed by April 2026. The study will be finished on 31 December 2029.

Cases and control subjects’ data will be collected at the above-mentioned seven sites. Each site aims to collect 40 individuals with chronic and constant tinnitus and 40 non-tinnitus control subjects. A group-matching will be obtained for sex, age and hearing loss between tinnitus and control subjects post recruitment. Participants will be screened and included in the study irrespective of race, ethnicity or gender. We will exclude participants that do not speak Dutch, English or German because not all screening forms, questionnaires and tests are available or validated in other languages. To participate in this study, subjects should be able to provide informed consent, have a confirmed chronic subjective tinnitus diagnosis for the tinnitus group and if receiving any tinnitus related treatment (pharmacological or non-pharmacological), the regimen must be stable for at least 6 months (no initiation or major change) and treatment history will be recorded. See figure 2 for overview. Inclusion criteria . (1) for tinnitus cases: a diagnosis of chronic tinnitus (for at least 6 months based on history) and constant, subjective, non-pulsatile tinnitus, classified as primary tinnitus and for controls: not experienced tinnitus for longer than 2 min in one instance; (2) age 18–70 years; (3) ability to understand and consent to the research; (4) ability to participate; (5) Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MOCA) test ≥26; (6) Hyperacusis Questionnaire (HQ) score ≤27 and (7) Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS) <14. (8) for tinnitus cases: a diagnosis of chronic tinnitus (for at least 6 months based on history) and constant, subjective, non-pulsatile tinnitus, classified as primary tinnitus and (9) for controls: not experienced tinnitus for longer than 2 min in one instance; To focus on chronic subjective tinnitus and reduce confounding from secondary/‘organic’ aetiologies and severe psychiatric or neurological disorders that can complicate differential diagnosis, we will apply the following exclusion criteria: (1) Objective tinnitus; heartbeat-synchronous tinnitus as primary concern; (2) otosclerosis; acoustic neuroma or other relevant ear disorders with fluctuating hearing; (3) acute ear nose and throat infections (acute otitis media, otitis externa, acute sinusitis); (4) Ménière’s disease or similar syndromes; (5) vestibular migraine; (6) serious internal, neurological or psychiatric conditions; (7) epilepsy or other central nervous system disorders (brain tumour, encephalitis); (8) clinically relevant drug, medication or alcohol abuse up to 2 weeks before study start; (9) severe hearing loss operationally defined as pure-tone audiometry (PTA) ≥71 dB hearing level (HL) in the better ear (average of 0.5, 1, 2 and 4 kHz); (10) inability to communicate properly in the course of the study; (11) one deaf ear.

Each site will be responsible for standard tinnitus assessments including the European School of Interdisciplinary Tinnitus-Survey Questionnaire (ESIT-SQ); the Tinnitus Handicap Inventory (THI, Cronbach’s alpha=0.93); the Tinnitus Functional Index (TFI, Cronbach’s alpha=0.97). Both cases and controls will complete the HADS (Cronbach’s alpha=0.83–0.85), the Perceived Stress Questionnaire (PSQ-30, Cronbach’s alpha=0.94); the HQ (Cronbach’s alpha=0.90) and some additional questions. Most of these have been previously tested and validated on a tinnitus sample. 23 Whenever possible, the questionnaires will be delivered on-line via Research Electronic Data Capture electronic data capture software. All questionnaires are validated for tinnitus research. The questionnaires are described below:
Audiological and/or tinnitus assessments will be conducted by responsible medical, audiology and/or trained study staff with a standard clinical audiometer.

In the event of an adverse occurrence, the participants will be asked to provide a detailed report including the severity of the event. Additionally, participants will be asked to indicate whether they believe the event is related to the study. If a participant decides to withdraw from the study, we will ask them to share the reason for their departure. This information will help us understand any potential issues and improve future research efforts.

All sites will collect evoked-related potentials (ERPs) with a 64-channel EEG cap. The site in Tübingen plans to simultaneously record MEG data in order to replicate findings from a pilot study on healthy participants. 32 However, this would be possible only owing to a low-interference of magnetic high-frequency ER2 earbuds (see https://www.interacoustics.com/images/research/pdf/8540345-ER-2_Earphones-v1-01-2024.pdf for more details) with the MEG sensors. In the event this cannot be achieved, only EEG data will be collected in Tübingen. Two test paradigms will be combined that are derived from the most recent models of tinnitus and which have shown promise in pilot studies. A first approach is based on a method used in animals to objectively assess tinnitus by gap detection, namely GPIAS . 33 34 The GPIAS paradigm is inspired by the combination of both gap detection and prepulse inhibition (PPI), used for the assessment of temporal sensory processing in both animals and humans. The basic principle of PPI relies on the ability of a weak lead stimulus (a prepulse or a silent gap presented in a carrier background) to inhibit a startling effect of a following, more intense, abrupt stimulus. These paradigms have been used to assess the automatic or preconscious inhibition of the motor reflex response that occurs in healthy subjects. Disruption in the inhibition caused by prepulses (either of different intensities above the carrier background, or at different interstimulus intervals (ISIs)) is a correlate of schizophrenia, while disruption of the inhibition by gaps (at specific carrier frequencies) is thought to underlie tinnitus. While there is substantial evidence in preclinical models that GPIAS deficits are associated with tinnitus, 35 its validation in humans using the blinking response has remained controversial. 36 Moreover, animals and humans with tinnitus can still consciously perceive the gap, even when the carrier would closely match the putative tinnitus. 37 Because GPIAS is regulated at the level of the auditory cortex, 38 40 cortical responses may provide a more accurate measure of inhibition than the traditional motor reflex responses. The hypothesis is that individuals with tinnitus would have impaired inhibition of cortical evoked responses to sound pulses when preceded by a silent gap embedded at a specific carrier frequency closely matching the tinnitus percept, in comparison to non-tinnitus individuals. Ongoing pilot studies suggest that silent gaps in a broadband noise (BBN) carrier can effectively suppress ERPs to 90 dB pulses in healthy participants, 32 which supports the notion that tinnitus would impair gap-mediated inhibition of the startle reflex, rather than ‘filling the gap’. A second approach is based on the concept that tinnitus occurrence is related to altered processing of prediction errors. 41 48 Predictive coding model is now widely gaining recognition and consensus to explain the integrated functioning of the brain. The theory is that the brain maintains an internal prediction model with which it compares the incoming sensory information to produce its perception of the environment around it. The difference between the prediction and the input is called a prediction error. If the error is large and strong, it modifies the internal model by changing the prediction and thereby the percept. This concept is supported by empirical evidence demonstrating that people with tinnitus exhibit a more pronounced electrophysiological response to a mismatch between predictions (the expected sound based on the auditory training paradigm) and perceptions as compared with non-tinnitus individuals. 42 This sensitivity to prediction errors (the difference between prediction and input) is associated with how loud patients perceive their tinnitus, independent of co-occurring hyperacusis and hearing loss. 42 For example, the amplitude of the mismatch negativity (MMN) positively correlates with subjectively reported tinnitus loudness. Thus, the MMN might be a biomarker for how loud tinnitus patients perceive their tinnitus. That is, people with a more pronounced electrophysiological response to a prediction error perceive a louder phantom sound. Using another paradigm, a group, independent of us, confirmed the importance of the MMN for tinnitus detection. 43 Furthermore, an increase in amplitude and a delay in latency for the late positive evoked brain response (P300) has been demonstrated in tinnitus patients using both auditory and visual oddball paradigms. Both the MMN and P300 are conceived as measures of prediction errors identified at respectively the sensory cortex and higher levels (ie, frontal-parietal cortex). 49 50 The P300 is thought to reflect processes involved in stimulus evaluation or categorisation; whether the stimulus is behaviourally relevant or not. Therefore, the aim of the current approach is to validate that both the MMN and the P300, using an auditory oddball paradigm with omission, can be used as biomarkers for tinnitus loudness and presence, respectively, (ie, cross-validation). We propose to investigate these two paradigms in a large international sample of tinnitus patients and controls in order to determine the sensitivity of GPIAS and the oddball paradigm in diagnosing tinnitus in humans.

After completing the questionnaires, the (M/E)EG recordings will be obtained in a quiet, dimmed room, with each participant sitting upright. Prior to GPIAS and the oddball paradigm, resting-state (5 min with open eyes) will be collected. The order of the GPIAS (see figure 3 ) and oddball paradigm (see figure 4 ) will be randomised between subjects for each site separately.

sections.section: Gap Prepulse Inhibition Of The Acoustic Startle
sections.text: Throughout, participants will be presented with a dark ‘+’ mark on a white background screen in order to maintain fixation. Sound will be calibrated directly from the ear insert to the calibration microphone and will be compared with a high frequency head calibrator for monitoring purposes. Sounds will be delivered binaurally through Etymotic ER2 ear inserts with a background sound pressure level (SPL) of <35 dB(A) SPL, thereafter shortened as dB. Broadband pulses (20 ms, 90 dB, no rise and fall time) will be presented in a continuous carrier BBN, or a 1 kHz-wide narrowband noise centred at 3 kHz or 8 kHz of 60 dB. Silent gaps (50 ms, 2 ms rise and fall ramp, down to background noise floor level) will precede a pulse by 240 ms ISI. Peak amplitude and latency of the N1 ERP will be measured in response to 2 ms long trials containing (1) pulse only (PO), (2) pulses preceded by silent gaps (GP), (3) or gap only (GO) will be recorded. PO, GP and GO trials are presented 100 times in trio blocks of random PO, GP, GO order within a specific carrier frequency range. Session of BBN will be tested, as well as Butterworth filtered 1 kHz-wide narrow band noises centred at 3 kHz and centred at 8 kHz (48 dB/octave). The order of these sessions will be randomised. Prior to and after these three sessions, 25 PO trials of various and randomised sound intensity levels (70, 75, 80, 85 and 90 dB) presented in 60 dB BBN will allow us to assess ERP input/output growth function (total 50 trials), as well as habituation to the pulses only. After each session, we will communicate with the participants via an intercom system making sure they are comfortable. The total duration of the GPIAS sessions will be around 1 hour.

ERPs in response to auditory stimuli will be collected from all participants following a procedure similar to Wacongne and coworkers. 51 Stimuli . The stimuli consist of three sets of auditory sequences with a combination of pure tones and white noise bursts. Sequence X will have five 500 Hz tones; Sequence Y will have four 500 Hz tones and one white noise burst; Sequence Omission will have four 500 Hz tones. The tones and noise bursts will be 50 ms long with a rise-fall time of 7 ms and ISI of 250 ms. The signal power of the tones and the noise bursts and the overall power of the sequences will be normalised to have the same root mean square power. Presentation levels . The stimuli will be presented at the most comfortable loudness level of the participant. This will be determined by first presenting Sequence Omission at a loudness level that is uncomfortable to the participant. The initial ‘uncomfortable’ level is determined individually during the session using the 1–7 loudness rating (one being very soft; 7=uncomfortably loud), starting from a clearly audible level based on the participant’s 500 Hz threshold and increasing in 5 dB steps until a rating of 7 is reached (or the participant requests termination; with an upper safety cap). The level is then reduced in 5 dB steps; the intended 30 dB range is used only if the lowest level remains audible. If a 30 dB decrement would fall below audibility for the participant, the decrement is reduced so that the minimum level remains above threshold (eg, ≥5–10 dB senstaion level (SL)). This will be repeated five times and participants will be asked to rate the sound on a scale of 1–7. The sound with an intensity rating of 4 will be considered their most comfortable loudness level. If there is more than one chosen level, the choices will be replayed, and the participants choose the sound that is their most comfortable loudness level. Following this, the participants will be asked to match the loudness of the four tones to that of the noise burst. The noise burst will be varied in loudness by 5 dB, similar to the above procedure. This time participants will be asked to rate the matching from 1 to 7 where a rating of 7 means that the loudness of the noise burst is ‘very loud compared to the other 4 tones’; rating of 1 means that the loudness of the noise burst is ‘very soft compared to the other 4 tones’. Here, a rating of 4 will mean a loudness match. The sequence that gets the most 4s will be chosen to be their Sequence Y. The most comfortable loudness level and the loudness matching between the tones and noise burst ensures that the differences in ERPs between the standard and deviants are not due to differences in subjective loudness perception between the two kinds of stimuli. Furthermore, it also controls for the amount of hearing loss in a more appropriate subjective way, where the perception of the loudness of a given intensity depends on the amount of hearing loss. Paradigm . The full session will consist of three protocols—(1) xxxxx protocol: Sequence X will be the standard, Sequence Y will be the first deviant and Sequence Omission will be the second deviant, (2) xxxxY protocol: Sequence Y will be the standard, Sequence X will be the first deviant and Sequence Omission will be the second deviant, (3) Omission-only protocol: Sequence Omission will be 100% expected. Each protocol consists of five blocks with 125 trials per block. Every block starts with 25 trials of the standard sequence in that protocol to establish the global rule. Of the next 100 trials, the standard will be randomly presented with 75% probability, deviant with 15% probability and omission sequence with 10% probability. In the omission-only protocol, 125 trials of Sequence Omission will be presented separately. Thus, in the five blocks per protocol, 500 standards, 75 deviants and 50 omission sequences will be presented for one protocol. A random intertrial jitter of 1300–1500 ms will be incorporated. Therefore, one trial will consist of the 5-stimulus sequence with an ISI of 250 ms and a random intertrial interval between 1300 and 1500 ms. The protocols will be presented in a randomised fashion between the xxxxx, xxxxY and omission-only protocols. Participants will be asked to always attend to the stimuli while keeping their eyes fixed on a point in front of them and will be allowed to take a break every two blocks and between subsequent protocols.

When using EEG or MEG recording, there exists a slight possibility of skin irritation. The area where the sensors make contact with the skin may appear red temporarily, typically dissipating within approximately 15 min. These issues may be mitigated through the meticulous selection of electrolyte, typically a basic salt solution such as potassium chloride and thorough disinfection of electrodes. There is a minimal risk using EEG in experiencing an electric shock from the sensors. Precautions to avoid this risk include the use of high-quality circuit breakers and isolation transformers, which effectively separate the equipment from the primary power source to ensure user safety. Consequently, the likelihood of encountering an electric shock tends towards zero. Repeated exposure to the sound paradigms may cause discomfort, in particular, for the GPIAS procedure, in individuals with tinnitus. For such reasons, the researchers will not be blinded during the acquisition on the participants. Nonetheless, pilot tests showed that 90 dB pulses are supported by both individuals with and without tinnitus (∼n=20) and give similar ERP amplitudes as 95 dB pulses. Likewise, 60 dB carriers are equally effective as the 65 dB ones and more comfortable. Therefore, 90 dB pulses in a 60 dB carrier will be considered here. Participants will be informed that the sessions may be terminated at any time in case of uncomfortable loudness. Given the non-invasive nature of EEG/MEG and psychoacoustic testing, serious adverse events are not expected. The most likely adverse events include transient scalp redness/itching or mild skin irritation from the EEG cap/electrolyte; transient discomfort due to sound stimulation (including startle or hyperacusis-related discomfort); fatigue and/or mild headache due to prolonged testing; transient dizziness/nausea; and (where applicable) anxiety/claustrophobia during MEG. To minimise these risks, electrodes will be applied using skin-friendly procedures (minimal abrasion; disinfected electrodes; hypoallergenic electrolyte where needed) and participants will be monitored throughout the session. Sound stimuli are delivered at calibrated, conservative levels and can be reduced or the session paused/terminated at the participant’s request. Regular breaks will be offered, and testing will stop immediately if the participant reports unacceptable discomfort. All adverse events will be recorded with severity and relatedness, and managed and reported according to local ethics/IRB procedures; participants will be advised to contact the study team if symptoms persist, and clinical follow-up will be arranged when indicated.

The study is designed to give us an adequate power to validate that the GPIAS and the oddball paradigm can be used as a biomarker for tinnitus loudness and presence. For GPIAS, we hypothesise decreased inhibition of the N1 pulse response when presenting a gap at specific carrier frequencies in the tinnitus group when compared with controls. We expect similar inhibition between cases and controls when using BBN. For the oddball paradigm, we expect tinnitus patients to show a stronger electrophysiological response to a mismatch between predictions and perceptions as well as an increase in amplitude and a delay in latency for the late positive evoked brain response in comparison to controls. We aim to collect approximately 40 cases and 40 controls per site, summing to 280 individuals per group, which would offer us a power of 80% to detect the difference between groups using Cohen’s f estimate for a small effect size (0.15). As this is not a longitudinal study, we do not expect attrition. Potential confounders that will be considered in the analysis are age, sex, hearing loss and hyperacusis, as these may differ between cases and controls. 11

All data will be managed using unique study codes, which will serve to encode and organise all electronic information, safeguarding participant confidentiality. The key associating these codes with participants’ identities will be securely stored in a protected file. Access to this key will be restricted solely to designated members of the research team at each site. To uphold privacy standards, all research documentation will be securely stored within locked file cabinets in secured offices. Electronic data will be housed on a secure, password-protected server and all corresponding data analysis will be conducted within individual study sites to ensure comprehensive and centralised data protection. Participant names will not be disclosed, and only summary statistics will be conducted on all variables and subsequently reported. Data collected for analysis will include: (1) demographics (age, sex/gender, race/ethnicity where available, study site and assessment language); (2) clinical characteristics (case/control status; tinnitus duration and characteristics from ESIT-SQ; treatment history and stability; MoCA; HQ; questionnaire measures including THI, TFI, HADS, PSQ-30; and VAS symptom ratings); (3) audiological measures (pure-tone thresholds including high frequencies derived hearing-loss indices such as PTA, and tinnitus pitch and loudness matching); and (4) neurophysiological outcomes derived from EEG/MEG. All variables will be stored under unique study codes with identifiers kept separately, and analyses will use de-identified coded data only.

The identification and validation of a biomarker for subjective tinnitus is considered a crucial step in the development of a personalised approach to the diagnosis and treatment of tinnitus. The objective of the TIDE consortium is to develop and validate an objective marker for chronic and constant subjective tinnitus. The development of a biomarker in tinnitus would advance patient management to a new level. European guidelines for the management of tinnitus have investigated the evidence for treatment interventions and concluded in 2018 that only for cognitive–behavioural therapy (CBT) there exists some evidence for treatment benefits, 52 yet these guidelines need updating to be in line with more recently developed evidence for other treatments. 53 However, whereas CBT helps patients coping with tinnitus—it does not suppress it, which according to many patient organisations is the primary requirement. 20 Overall, despite a high societal need, research on tinnitus has been poorly funded, 54 pharmacological interventions failed to provide evidence of treatment benefits 55 and the pipeline for drug development remains thin. 56 European funding incentives such as the ESIT, 57 Tinnitus Assessment Causes and Treatments and Unification of Treatments and Interventions for Tinnitus Patients 58 have helped in providing a basis for further developments, but more is needed. Recent treatment innovations such as notch music therapy, 59 direct vagus nerve stimulation 60 61 and bimodal stimulation 62 63 have raised hopes for tinnitus patients, but primary outcome measures still rely on subjective assessments with questionnaires, 26 and minimal clinically important difference levels that are not always consistent. 64 Despite the use of different assessment methods between preclinical research and clinical trials, research overall supports the translational potential of animal research. GPIAS, which is used for the assessment of tinnitus in animals, has been inspired by prepulse inhibition, a validated measure of temporal processing that has been used for nearly half a century for understanding the mechanisms underlying complex disorders like schizophrenia. GPIAS relies on an objective reflex response that has been validated against conditional behavioural paradigms 33 34 and various neural correlates. 65 67 However, because GPIAS shares resemblance with gap detection, a subjective test used for the assessment of auditory gating, it has been criticised and misunderstood. Animals and humans with tinnitus can subjectively ‘detect’ this silent gap, even when the carrier frequency closely matches that of the perceived tinnitus. 37 68 However, cumulative evidence points towards a rapid subconscious inhibitory mechanism. While both PPI and GPIAS relay their motor reflex mechanisms via the inferior colliculus and the caudal pontine reticular nucleus, PPI is relayed in the lateral globus pallidus and GPIAS is mediated in the auditory cortex. 39 Elegant optogenetic experiments in mice have evidenced that inhibitory interneurons in the auditory cortex are sensitive to the sound offset and onset, overall involving a comparison of pregap and postgap spiking activity to regulate the inhibition of the motor reflex to a pulse stimulus. 40 Although the mechanisms underlying the poorer inhibition happening in animals with tinnitus at specific frequencies are not clearly understood, we hypothesise that it may involve an interference with the ability of interneurons in the auditory cortex to properly inhibit the startle response. GPIAS tests based on the blinking reflex response in humans with tinnitus using the electro-oculographic response failed to provide strong test–retest reliability. 36 Pilot studies from TIDE have shown that inhibition measures with the MEG are 50 times less variable than electrooculography (EOG), and thus would plausibly offer a more reliable comparison between tinnitus and non-tinnitus controls. Alterations in error prediction have also been postulated as a relevant mechanism for tinnitus generation, with changes to this predictive coding system measured using neurophysiology. 41 4869 Particularly, sensory oddball tasks probe different features of the predictive coding network and characterise them in different components of the neural response. Oddball paradigms usually consist of a standard stimulus that is randomly interspersed with a deviant stimulus, which being novel elicits a surprise. One of the theories behind this is that the brain records a temporary memory trace of the standard (which can be hypothesised to be the prediction) and the difference between the response of the deviant and the standard is the prediction error. 50 Oddball paradigms produce early and late components in infants and adults that record changes in sensory and cognitive processes. MMN is a frontocentral negativity occurring around 100–200 ms poststimulus presentation 70 that is known to encode prediction errors. 71 In infants, pitch, 72 73 timing, 74 75 and deviants in melodies 76 create mismatch responses showing a very early sign of encoding prediction errors. 69 Furthermore, MMN components change after only a few hours of exposure, reflecting learning. 69 77 For a long time, it was debated that MMN responses represented neural adaptation patterns given that they were recorded in response to changes in stimulus characteristics. 78 However, more recent studies in both adult humans and monkeys show that MMNs generated by the omission of a stimulus in a sequence cannot be explained by neural adaptation and are a reliable marker to prediction errors. 50 69 79 While MMNs record sensory prediction errors, changes in cognitive components and more complex processes such as updating of sensory memory occur later in time. In infants, an increase in a late positive component between 700 and 1000 ms called the positive slow wave (PSW) 80 is traditionally considered a marker representing the updating of memory specifically in response to partially encoded infrequent stimuli. 69 81 82 The PSW is also considered an early precursor of the P300 component observed in adults in response to oddball paradigms. 81 83 Although the P300 is usually recorded to the target and novelty stimulus its credibility to be a marker for prediction error is gaining traction. 42 50 69 TIDE will determine the reliability of GPIAS and the oddball paradigm across several clinical sites. In conclusion, the value of an objective, robust biomarker would be transformative in tinnitus treatment, including risk reduction associated with inappropriate treatment regimen or inability to detect an efficacy signal rapidly. Discovering and confirming a biomarker associated with tinnitus is considered a pivotal stage in advancing personalised methods for diagnosing this condition. In conclusion, this clinical study will enhance our understanding of the neurobiological background of tinnitus by directly testing two candidate mechanisms derived from contemporary tinnitus models. By determining whether these biomarkers track tinnitus presence and/or perceived intensity—and whether they vary systematically with key clinical features (eg, hearing loss, hyperacusis, distress)—the project will help resolve ongoing uncertainty about which brain processes are most closely linked to tinnitus generation and maintenance, versus those reflecting comorbidities or general auditory dysfunction. Importantly, identifying robust, reproducible neurophysiological signatures (even if limited to specific subgroups) would support a more mechanistically grounded phenotyping of tinnitus, shifting the field away from trial-and-error management toward a data-driven framework that can better guide stratification in clinical trials and accelerate translational progress.
